Please do not define bitfields conditional on target endianness for wire-format data. Bitfield bit-ordering is implementation defined, see section `[class.bit]` in N4950 (C++23 draft specification):

> Allocation of bit-fields within a class object is implementation-defined. Alignment of bit-fields is implementation-defined.

Shifts and masks in host endianness don't rely on implementation specifics and are thus better practice. However, to use them you must deal with any endianness concerns prior to extracting the field member. As the type is uint8_t here, there are no concerns with endianness anyway, so it's just a straight shift/mask concern.

why not use the boost handlers for this? something along the lines of

struct sockaddr_mctp addr; // do your initialization
boost::asio::generic::datagram_protocol::endpoint ep(&addr, sizeof(addr), AF_MCTP);

and later, 

sock.send_to(reqMsg.data(), reqMsg.size(), ep);

That way you don't have to worry about weirdness around size differences between the sockaddr_mctp and the storage type sockaddr, boost will take care of it for you.

You may also want to consider using the non blocking version of this call so your thread can do meaningful work while this is being sent. This may require copying of same data, but for many mctp packets, copying data that's potentially already in the cache is quite cheap, especially compared to blocking io.

so in the timeout case here, considering the following flow:
1. Client sends a message
2. it times out, we give callback to the client.
3. Client sends another message
4. response for first message comes in, before the response of the second
5. We cancel the timer of the first response.
6. response for the second message never comes in
7. No timeout for the second message.
8. effective deadlock as we never get a callback for the second message, so the state machine never moves forward.

Am I missing something here?

This commit isn't about covering every edge case possible, but to implement something simple as suggested bu Ed. To handle such cases more enhanced MctpRequest is being introduce with the patch https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/dbus-sensors/+/80023.

I don't think this is an edge case as much as just the timeout behavior, which we've explicitly coded into this class. Why would we make a class with a known potential deadlock and then augment it with the proper behavior in a different commit (or class)? We may as well just completely remove the timeout behavior from this commit rather than half support something that will be difficult to debug when it goes wrong. As it stands, we have a known bug in the commit.

I think expected sequence would be

1. Client sends a message
2. it times out, we give callback to the client.
3. Client sends another message
4. response for first message comes in, before the response of the second
5. We cancel the timer of the first response. (This would not happen. Why do we cancel the timer of the first response? We would cancel the timer of the Second request itself and deadlock would never happen. Timer for the first request is already expired and its expiry callback is already invoked, that where the step 2 is executed.)

1) Ack
2) Timer is no longer armed as it expired, callback was called.
3) Timer is re-armed in handleSendMsgCompletion. Request has been sent.
4) Ack
5) Timer is cancelled - there is just one timer (so correlation to first/second response doesn't apply; we are not doing queueing of messages in this patch)
6) Ack
7) Ack, timer was not armed post 5).
8) We don't get deadlocked/blocked here. Client will continue to send messages when the sensor poll timer (a different) expires.

Am I missing something?

```
Whenever a reference is bound to a temporary object or to a subobject thereof, the lifetime of the temporary object is extended to match the lifetime of the reference (check temporary object lifetime exceptions), where the temporary object or its subobject is denoted by one of following expression:

a prvalue expression of an object type,
(until C++17)
a temporary materialization conversion,
(since C++17)
a parenthesized expression (e), where e is one of these expressions,
a built-in subscript expression of form a[n] or n[a], where a is an array and is one of these expressions,
a class member access expression of form e.m, where e is one of these expressions and m designates a non-static data member of object type,
a pointer-to-member operation of form e.*mp, where e is one of these expressions and mp is a pointer to data member,
a const_cast, static_cast, dynamic_cast, or reinterpret_cast conversion without a user-defined conversion that converts one of these expressions to the glvalue refers to the object designated by the operand, or to its complete object or a subobject thereof (an explicit cast expression is interpreted as a sequence of these casts),
a conditional expression of form cond ? e1 : e2 that is a glvalue, where e1 or e2 is one of these expressions, or
a built-in comma expression of form x, e that is a glvalue, where e is one of these expressions.
```
